title: Police use Taser on violent patient at Hotel Dieu
article: Police used a stun gun to subdue a psychiatric patient who had damaged a hospital room and assaulted a nurse.
The man, who stands six-foot-four and weighs about 350 pounds, was a patient Hotel Dieu Hospital.
He had become increasingly violent on the weekend, threatening staff, damaging a hospital room and shoving a nurse.
On Tuesday, the hospital asked police to arrest the man.
Staff couldn't restrain the massive patient, so they lured him into an elevator that had been temporarily closed and called the Kingston Police emergency response unit.
When officers tried to negotiate with the man, he refused to leave the elevator and became agitated, police spokesman Mike Weaver said yesterday.
Officers pepper-sprayed the man, but it had no effect. That was when one of the officers shot the man with a Taser.
The device delivers 50,000 volts of electricity for up to five seconds, enough to temporarily paralyse a person's muscles.
The man fell to his knees long enough for police to grab and handcuff him.
He was examined at the hospital and taken to court for a bail hearing Tuesday afternoon.
He was then taken to Quinte Detention Centre in Napanee until a court appearance by video tomorrow.
Police withheld the man's name because of his mental-health issues.
No one was injured in the arrest, but the growing use of Tasers by police is controversial.

Amnesty International recently renewed its call for police in the United States and Canada to stop using the device, which the organization says has been linked to nearly 80 deaths in North America since 2000.
Six people died last year after being shot with Tasers, although none of the deaths was attributed to the stun gun.
They include Samuel Truscott, a 43-year-old Kingston man who died in August after police used a Taser on him.
An autopsy found that Truscott died from a cocaine-induced heart attack.
But police say the stun guns are a much safer way to take down a dangerous suspect whom they might otherwise be forced to shoot with a pistol.
Not only are Tasers safe, they should be used by more police departments, Ontario deputy chief coroner Dr. Jim Cairns told an inquest underway in London into the death of Peter Lamonday.
The London man was shot with a Taser last May while in police custody.

A study for the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police came to a similar conclusion. It found that the Taser, used correctly, "has a very, very low probability of causing ventricular fibrillation," said author Steve Palmer, of the Canadian Police Research Centre.
